<info> The autism community website Wrong Planet was started in 2004 by American high school students Dan Grover and Alex Plank.[665]
<info> The British autism research charity Autistica was founded in 2004 by German-British software entrepreneur Dame Stephanie Shirley.[666]
<info> Autism Korea [KO] (한국자폐인사랑협회는) was founded in South Korea in January 2006.[667] It has focused on representing autistic people and their parents.
<info> Israeli people-with-autism representative organisation The community of people on the autistic spectrum in Israel [HE] began in early 2006.

<info> The UK's Autism Education Trust was established by the National Autistic Society and the UK's Department for Children, Schools and Families in 2007.[668][669] It is tasked with ensuring that all British children with autism are educated appropriately, through better education of their teachers.

<info> The Association of Professional Behavior Analysts was founded in the United States in 2007, to serve "the unique needs of professional practitioners."[670] It has since expanded its operations into other countries.

<info> The Autism Science Foundation was founded in the United States in April 2009, by Americans (and mothers of autistic children) Alison Singer (businessperson) and Karen London.[649] Its founders broke away from Autism Speaks due to its focus on funding research into possible links between vaccines and autism.
<info> Also in 2009, the Council on Autism Services was formed by 10 American autism service providers. The organisation was reformed as the "Council of Autism Service Providers" in 2015.[671]
<info> A popular book of 1998 was sensory processing guide The Out-of-Sync Child[672] by American music and movement teacher Carol Stock Kranowitz.[673] New editions were published in 2005 and 2022.
<info> The Introvert Advantage: How to Thrive in an Extrovert World was a popular book released by American psychologist Marti Olsen Laney[674] in February 2002.[675]

<info> August 2002 saw the publishing of Freaks, Geeks, and Asperger Syndrome: A User Guide to Adolescence by 13-year-old British adolescent with Asperger syndrome, Luke Jackson. The book was praised by Sula Wolff.[269] In January 2004, Luke and his family featured in the BBC documentary feature My Family and Autism.[676] In 2005, a fictional movie based on the family, Magnificent 7,[677] was aired on the BBC. It included a character based on Luke's mother, fellow autistic subject author Jacqui Jackson.

<info> Another book first published in August 2002 was A Parent's Guide to Asperger Syndrome and High-Functioning Autism by American psychologist Sally Ozonoff.[678] A second edition, A Parent's Guide to High-Functioning Autism Spectrum Disorder: How to Meet the Challenges and Help Your Child Thrive, was published in 2014 by Ozonoff and fellow American psychologists, Geraldine Dawson and James C. McPartland.[679] Over 125,000 copies of the books have been printed.

<info> Raising a Sensory Smart Child was first released in March 2005 by two Americans, the occupational therapist Lindsey Biel and the writer Nancy Peske.[680] New editions were released in 2009 and 2018.[681]

<info> Ten Things Every Child with Autism Wishes You Knew[682] was first published by American speech therapist Ellen Notbohm[683] in 2005. New editions were published in 2012 and 2019. Over 250,000 copies have been sold.

<info> ABA book The Verbal Behavior Approach: How to Teach Children With Autism and Related Disorders was released in May 2007 by two Americans, nurse Mary Barbera[684] and writer Tracy Rasmussen.[685]
<info> Released in September 2007 was the book Louder Than Words: A Mother's Journey in Healing Autism by American mother Jenny McCarthy.

<info> Smart but Scattered: The Revolutionary "Executive Skills" Approach to Helping Kids Reach Their Potential[686] was released in January 2009. Written by American psychologists Peg Dawson and Richard Guare, it has over 375,000 copies in print.
<info> Disconnected Kids was released by American neurologist Robert Melillo in January 2009.[687]
<info> Aspergirls: Empowering Females with Asperger Syndrome was published by American writer Rudy Simone in 2010. She went on to write a number of other books on autistic subjects.

<info> Emotional control guidebook Zones of Regulation[688] was published by American occupational therapist Leah Kuypers in 2011, to help autistic people and others who needed it. It has since sold over 100,000 copies.[689] Various other products helping people understand and use the Zones concept have since been created.

<info> Understanding Your Child's Sensory Signals: A Practical Daily Use Handbook for Parents and Teachers was released in September 2011 by American occupational therapist Angie Voss.[690] Two further editions have subsequently been published.
<info> The software program The Social Express[691] was first released in November 2011,[692] by American parents of autistic children Marc Zimmerman[693] and Tina Zimmerman.[694]
<info> Bestselling book Quiet: The Power of Introverts in a World That Can't Stop Talking was published by American writer Susan Cain in January 2012.

<info> The Survival Guide for Kids with Autism Spectrum Disorders (And Their Parents) was released in March 2012 by Americans Elizabeth Verdick (a writer)[695] and Elizabeth Reeve (a psychiatrist).[696] A new edition was released in 2021.[697]

<info> Denver Early Start Model book, An Early Start for Your Child with Autism: Using Everyday Activities to Help Kids Connect, Communicate, and Learn was released by Americans Sally J. Rogers, Geraldine Dawson and Laurie A. Vismara[698] in May 2012. It has sold over 100,000 copies.

<info> The Asperkids' (Secret) Book of Social Rules: The Handbook of Not-So-Obvious Guidelines for Teens and Tweens was published by American social worker Jennifer Cook in September 2012. It sold many copies, and won the Autism Society of America's Temple Grandin Outstanding Literary Work of the Year. Cook later write a number of other books about autism.
Other popular books and other media were published during this period, most notably the following:

<info> Personal memoir Nobody Nowhere: The Extraordinary Autobiography of an Autistic Girl by Australian Donna Williams was published in 1992, and was on the New York Times Bestsellers list in 1993.[699]
<info> The Hollywood action movie Mercury Rising (1998) featured an autistic boy.

<info> Pretending to Be Normal: Living with Asperger's Syndrome was an autobiography published by American researcher Liane Holliday Willey in 1999. She also coined the term aspie.[700] She released an updated edition in 2014. (The book was praised by Sula Wolff).[269] She went on to write a number of other books on autism topics.

<info> The book The Fear of Game Brain (ゲーム脳の恐怖) was released by Japanese physiologist Akio Mori in 2002, and sold over 100,000 copies in Japan. In a related speaking engagement, Mori was believed to say that autism is at least in part caused by people spending too much time playing video games. However, Mori refuted this assertion to Autism Society Japan.[701]

<info> The British fiction book The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time was published in May 2003 by Mark Haddon. It features a protagonist that the publishers have said has Asperger's syndrome, but was not specifically written that way. In 2012, it was made into a successful West End play, which then went to Broadway in 2014.

<info> The Flemish fiction book Nothing Was All He Said about a teenage boy with Asperger's syndrome was released by Belgian author Nic Balthazar in 2003. He would later direct the story as the movie Ben X, which was released in September 2007. (The movie was later remade in Sweden in 2013 as IRL).
<info> Mozart and the Whale, an American romantic comedy-drama film about two people with Asperger's syndrome, was first released in September 2005. It was based on a true story.
<info> The documentary feature Normal People Scare Me: A Film About Autism was produced by American actor Joey Travolta in 2006.

<info> The popular photo-book All Cats have Asperger Syndrome was released in October 2006 by Australian teacher Kathy Hoopmann.[702] A second edition (retitled All Cats have Autism) was released in 2020. She also wrote other books about autism and related conditions.

<info> Bestselling memoir The Reason I Jump was published in 2007. It is attributed to Naoki Higashida, a Japanese 13-year-old boy with autism. It was released in English in 2013, and has been translated into over 30 languages.

<info> Another popular book of 2007 was Look Me in the Eye: My Life with Asperger's by American John Elder Robison, first released in September that year. Robison would later become a board member of Autism Speaks.
<info> Children of the Stars (来自星星的孩子) is a 2007 documentary about lives of autistic children in China.

<info> The documentary movie Elle s'appelle Sabine [fr] (Her Name is Sabine) was screened at the Cannes Film Festival in May 2007. It was made by Sabine's sister, the French actress Sandrine Bonnaire. It won the Globe de Cristal for Best Documentary in 2008.

<info> The character Sheldon Cooper first appeared on American television in September 2007, in the popular sitcom The Big Bang Theory. While he is not explicitly autistic, according to the actor who plays him as an adult, the character "could not display more traits" of Asperger's syndrome.[703][704] (The character would later be the protagonist of the series Young Sheldon.)
<info> Popular autobiography Born On A Blue Day: Inside the Extraordinary Mind of an Autistic Savant was released by its British author Daniel Tammet in October 2007.
<info> The American dramatist Michael Golamco's short play Please Stand By is centred on an autistic woman, and was first staged in 2008. In 2017 it became the movie Please Stand By.
<info> The 2008 Swiss film Jimmie [de] was about a teenage boy with autism.
<info> The soap opera Aapki Antara first went on air in India in June 2009. The title character of the series is an autistic girl.
<info> The American film Adam was about a young man with Asperger's syndrome. It was released in July 2009.
<info> The 2011 documentary Le Mur (The Wall) challenged the extensive use of psychoanalysis in treating autism in France. It was made by French director Sophie Robert [fr].

<info> Histoire de l'autisme : de l'enfant sauvage aux troubles envahissants du développement[155] was written by French psychoanalyst and psychiatrist Jacques Hochmann [fr], and was released in January 2009.

<info> A history of autism: a conversation with the pioneers[705] was released in October 2010 by British autism researcher Adam Feinstein,[706] having been commissioned by Autistica founder Dame Stephanie Shirley.

In 2013, the DSM-5 eliminated Asperger's disorder as a separate diagnosis, instead considering autism to be a spectrum disorder referred to as autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Both in the research community and among autistic people, there is ongoing debate about whether autism should be considered a disorder, or whether it should be thought of as merely a different way of being.

In May 2013, the DSM-5 was released. It combined "autistic disorder", "Asperger's disorder", "CDD" and "PDD-NOS" into the broader concept of "autism spectrum disorder" (ASD), and discontinued the four earlier conditions. It also grouped the symptoms of ASD into two groups - impaired social communication and/or interaction, and restricted and/or repetitive behaviors.[707] The new definition was narrower than the collective definitions of its DSM-IV predecessors had been, reducing the number of neurodivergent people covered by it. One study found 10-40% of people covered by the immediately previous definitions were not covered by that in the DSM-5.[708]

The DSM-5 assigned three "severity levels" for ASD, with people in level 1 "requiring support", level 2 "requiring substantial support" and level 3 "requiring very substantial support".[709] Some autism activists believe the autistic spectrum should not be measured in this way, as it does not take into account the greatly varying attributes the people in the different DSM severity levels have, or that support needs can be context-dependent.[710][711]

DSM publishers, the American Psychiatric Association, said that "The revised diagnosis represents a new, more accurate, and medically and scientifically useful way of diagnosing individuals with autism-related disorders." It also noted that the conditions that the new ASD condition replaced "were not consistently applied across different clinics and treatment centers".[712]

A new condition of social (pragmatic) communication disorder (SCD) was added. This does not apply to people who fulfil all of the ASD criteria, but to those who only have the social communication difficulties found in the ASD definition. (It drew on the earlier concepts of "semantic pragmatic disorder" and "pragmatic language impairment.")
Another new condition was avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID). A 2023 study found that 21% of autistic people had ARFID features.[713]
"Schizoid personality disorder", "avoidant personality disorder" and "selective mutism" remained.

Another major change in this edition of the DSM was allowing individuals to be diagnosed with both ASD and ADHD. Previously, under the DSM's rules people could only be diagnosed as having one of their antecedent conditions. There is evidence to suggest that a majority of people with ASD also have ADHD.[714]

Similarly, people diagnosed with ASD could now also be diagnosed with other commonly co-morbid psychiatric syndromes such as social anxiety disorder, oppositional defiant disorder and developmental coordination disorder.

January 2022 saw the first official use of the ICD-11 (it having been released in 2019). This version of the ICD combined all PDD conditions as "autistic spectrum disorder" (following the DSM's practice). However, unlike the DSM-5, the ICD-11 included a number of ASD subdivisions.[715] Apart from an "other" and an "unspecified" category, these subdivisions were differentiated by two factors: "disorder of intellectual development" and impairment of "functional language."
As with the DSM-5, it now also allowed for dual-diagnosis of ASD with similar conditions.

Though it had been conceptualised and had become popular with autistic people much earlier, the concept of autistic masking (autistic people hiding their autistic natures through suppressing or replacing behaviours) became a focus of academic research in the 2010s.[716]: 18  Such masking often requires an exceptional mental effort,[717][718] leading to cognitive overload. This is a main cause of burnout in autistic people.[719][720] It is also linked with other adverse mental health outcomes.[721][722][723][724]
A diagnostic test called the "Aspie Quiz" was released by Swedish researcher Leif Ekblad[725] in July 2013.[726][727]

A December 2013 published study found that the brains of children with Asperger syndrome produced (on average) 42% more information when at rest, compared to non-ASD children.[728] It was conducted by Spanish-Canadian biochemist and biophysicist Jose Luis Perez-Velazquez,[729] and Spanish-American neuroscientist Roberto Fernández Galán.[730]
The Review Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders[731] was established in the United States by Springer in March 2014.[732]

Autism Speaks, Hospital for Sick Children (Toronto) and Google Genomics began the AUT10K project in 2014.[733] It created one of the world's largest collections of autism related genetic material, and had open access to researchers, called AGRE. The project later evolved into the similar MSSNG project. MSSNG aims to "provide the best resources to enable the identification of many subtypes of autism".[734] The MSSNG project was quickly met with criticism from autistic self-advocates.[735]

"Synaptic, transcriptional and chromatin genes disrupted in autism" was a well-cited paper published in October 2014.[736] The study investigated thousands of people with autism, and identified the gene mutations involved. The paper's lead authors were the Americans Joseph Buxbaum (neuroscientist) and Mark Daly (geneticist).
Brazilian researcher Alysson Muotri and others founded the company Tismoo in 2015, which aims to develop genetic treatments for autism and other conditions.[737]
The journal Advances in Autism[738] was launched by British publisher Emerald Publishing in July 2015.[739]

The term aphantasia (an inability to picture something in one's mind), was first published by British neurologist Adam Zeman, British neuropsychologist Michaela Dewar,[740] and Italian-British neuroscientist Sergio Della Sala in December 2015.[741] (The phenomenon was first described by British polymath Francis Galton in 1880.)[742] A 2021 study led by British psychologist Carla Dance[743] found that people with aphantasia had higher levels of autistic symptoms than controls.[744][745][746] A later Australasian study did not find such a correlation, and noted that many autistic people are visual thinkers.[747]
The open access journal Autism & Developmental Language Impairments[748] was launched by American publisher Sage Journals in January 2016.

The as-yet untested hypothesis of "RCCX Theory" was first self-published in February 2016[749] by American psychiatrist and internal medicine physician Sharon Meglathery.[750] It posits that genetic variations in the RCCX cluster lead to a cluster of comorbid autism, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) and other conditions.[749] Others have also considered parts of this cluster.[751] The theory gained greater prominence in September 2024.[752]

An October 2016 paper by three researchers from the University of York examined Asperger syndrome as "an alternative prosocial adaptive strategy" which may have developed as a result of the emergence of "collaborative morality" in the context of small-scale hunter-gathering, i.e. where "a positive social reputation for making a contribution to group wellbeing and survival" becomes more important than complex social understanding.[753]
The concept of autistic burnout became much more common on Twitter in 2017–18, and subsequently attracted more academic research.[754]

French neuroscientist Mohamed Jaber[755] found that the brain's motor fronto-striatal and cerebellar systems were major sites of autistic brain difference, and published about it in an April 2017 paper.[756]
A study by American psychologist Henny Kupferstein[757] published in January 2018 found that autistics who had been given ABA therapy were 86% more likely to have PTSD than those who had not.[758]

The well-cited study "Prevalence of Autism Spectrum Disorder Among Children Aged 8 Years — Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring Network, 11 Sites, United States, 2014"[759] was released in April 2018 by 26 US-based authors led by epidemiologist Jon Baio.[760] It found that one in 59 US children aged 8 years had ASD (nearly 2%). It also found that 56% of autistic children had an intellectual disability (with an IQ of 85 or less), and 44% had IQ scores in the average to above average range.
A National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorders in Australia was released by Autism CRC in August 2018.[761]
The journal Autism in Adulthood was launched by American publisher Mary Ann Liebert, Inc. in March 2019.
The Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire (CAT-Q) was released by British psychologist Laura Hull,[762] Simon Baron-Cohen and others in March 2019.[763] It measured autistic masking.

Another March 2019 published study found that microbiota transfer therapy was an effective treatment for autistic symptoms.[764] The lead author was Korean-American environmental engineer Dae-Wook Kang.[765]

The well cited paper "Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder" was published in January 2020.[766] It was a wholistic primer on child autism for doctors. The lead author was American paediatrician Susan L. Hyman.[767]

An ABA tool, the graduated electric decelarator, became the third device ever banned by the United States' Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in March 2020.[768] Its main user, the Judge Rotenberg Center, filed a lawsuit against the FDA, and in July 2021, the DC Circuit Court overturned the ban, meaning that the centre can still use the device.[769][770]
The report Interventions for children on the autism spectrum: A synthesis of research evidence was released by the Autism CRC in November 2020.[771] It compared dozens of different interventions.

A January 2022 published study by Catherine Lord and others introduced the concept of profound autism.[772][773] It refers to autistic people that have no or minimal verbal language, and/or an IQ less than 50. The "profound" refers to the perpetual access to a carer that adults with the condition require, noting that "profound autism is thus defined not by autistic features but by intellectual or language disability." A 2023 CDC study found that 27% of American 8 year olds with autism had this condition.[774]
American psychiatrist Lynn Kern Koegel[775] became the sixth editor of the Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders in 2022. She and her husband had earlier developed pivotal response treatment.
The concept of the pebbling social behaviour became defined by 2022.[citation needed]
The Autistic Burnout construct screening test for burnout in autistic people was released in May 2023.[776] It was developed by American psychologist Jared Richards[777] and twelve others.[778]

An August 2024 published study found that male mouse foetuses with low aromatase activity were more likely to develop autism symptoms post-birth, and this likelihood could be increased by maternal BPA exposure. It also found a connection between maternal BPA exposure and male child autism in humans.[779][780][781] The study was led by Singaporean-Australian biochemist Wah Chin Boon[782] and Australian epidemiologist Anne-Louise Ponsonby.[783]
Autism CRC released the National Framework for assessing children's functional strengths and support needs in Australia in December 2024.[784]

In July 2025, a team led by Russian-American computer scientist Olga Troyanskaya published that they had found four biologically distinct autism subtypes with differing comorbidities and symptoms.[785][786] The four subtypes were:
<info> Moderate challenges (low impact of the seven autism symptom factors measured)
<info> Broadly affected (high impact of all factors, frequent co-occurring conditions (particularly OCD, seizures/epilepsy and tics), very high rate of intellectual disability)
<info> Social and/or behavioural (low impact of developmental delay, and frequent co-occurring OCD, tics, ADHD, anxiety, seizures/epilepsy and major depression, high rate of intellectual disability)
<info> Mixed ASD with developmental delay (low impact of mood symptoms and disruptive behaviour, frequent co-occurring seizures/epilepsy, very high rate of intellectual disability)

In September 2025, US President Donald Trump,[787][788] the US Department of Health and Human Services[789] and the US Food and Drug Administration[790] announced that paracetamol (acetaminophen) use should be avoided by pregnant mothers due to it being a cause of autism, and that it is also better for an unborn baby than their mother running a high fever. Many other health authorities believed the autism-inducing effects to be less than warned.[791][792][793][794][795]

Simultaneously, it was announced that leucovorin was to be begin the US government approval process for treating cerebral folate deficiency, which was said to be a cause of autistic symptoms in some people.[787][789][796]

In October 2025, a team led by the psychiatry researchers Xinhe Zhang[797] (Chinese-British) and Varun Warrier[798] (Indian-British) published that they had found two biologically distinct autism subtypes. One is a typically early-diagnosed condition that includes significant childhood communication difficulties. The other is typically later-diagnosed, involving significant adolescent social difficulties, and has significant overlap with ADHD, depression, and PTSD.[799][800]
The Iran Autism Association was founded in 2013 by treatment professionals along with autistics and their families.[801]

Also in 2013, the French single mother "Rachel" had her three children taken from her by the government. They claimed that the children were mistreated, as evidenced by their unusual behaviour. Rachel claimed that their behaviour was due to autism and other conditions, but the government health authorities disagreed. It was subsequently determined that two of the three children had autism (with the other having ADHD), and that the mother herself had Asperger's syndrome.[802][803][804] The matter gained great publicity in France, being known as the "Affaire Rachel [fr]".[805]

The United States government passed the Autism CARES Act of 2014, authorising the spending of US$1.3 billion between 2015 and 2019. This extended the work of the Combating Autism Act. The Act was reauthorised in 2019.

The "Autism Navigator" website[806] for parents and clinicians of children that have or are suspected of having autism, was launched in April 2015 by Florida State University.[807][808] It is highly regarded by the American Academy of Pediatrics.[766]

The first Social Communication Intervention Programme (SCIP)[809] manual was published in 2015 by British speech and language therapist Catherine Adams.[810] SCIP was based on research she and others had conducted since 2005.[811] The program teaches social communication skills to children. It involves social understanding and social interpretation, pragmatics and language processing.[812][813]
Emotion-recognition teaching game "EmotiPlay"[814][815][816] was first developed in 2015[817] by Israeli educational software company Compedia [he].[818]
In October 2015, representative body Autism Canada was created through the merger of Autism Society Canada and Autism Canada Foundation.[352]
2016 saw Australia's main state-based and other autism representative organisations group together as the Australian Autism Alliance.[819]

The Hidden Disabilities Sunflower program was established in 2016 by London's Gatwick Airport, in consultation with two autism support groups and other disability advocates. It soon spread across the UK, and later to other developed countries.[820]
In March 2017, the Russian peak parents-of-autistic-children representative body Autism Regions (Аутизм Регионы)[821] was founded.[822]

Neurodiversity employment services organisation Untapped Group[823] was co-founded by Australian accountant Andrew Eddy in 2017.[824] It operates in the United States and Australia, and notably organises the prominent Autism at Work[825] conferences.

The ABA Coding Coalition greatly changed US prescription practice to fund more ABA treatment of autistic people on 1 January 2019.[826] It did this by convincing the American Medical Association to class ABA as a proven effective treatment in the government mandated Current Procedural Terminology coding system, while previously it was classed as only having some evidence of efficacy.[827] This meant that US health insurance companies now had to fund prescribed ABA for their clients, when previously they could contest it.[827] (The Coalition was made up of the Association of Professional Behavior Analysts, Autism Speaks, and the Behavior Analyst Certification Board).[826]
Also in the United States in January 2019, the National Council on Severe Autism was founded.[828] It is concerned with autistic people who have an IQ of 85 or less.[829]
The Blue Envelope Program helps US police understand how autistic people behave, and vice versa.[830] It began operating in January 2020.[831]
Australia's National Disability Insurance Scheme went into full operation in 2020. It provides many autistic people in that country with substantial amounts of money to help them live fuller lives.
In April 2021, America's Autism Awareness Month became Autism Acceptance Month.[832]
Global online support organisation the "Stimpunks Foundation" was established in the United States in December 2021, by IT workers Ryan Boren and Inna Boren.[833]
The National Guideline for Supporting the Learning, Participation, and Wellbeing of Autistic Children and Their Families in Australia was released by Autism CRC in February 2023.[834][835]
The first autistic Barbie doll was released in January 2026. It was developed with the assistance of ASAN.[836][837][838]
<info> British singer Susan Boyle mentioned in a December 2013 interview that she had been diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome.[839]
<info> Swedish activist Greta Thunberg's mother told a national newspaper of her daughter's Asperger's diagnosis in May 2015.[840] Greta would become globally prominent as an activist in 2018.
<info> British actor Anthony Hopkins mentioned in a January 2017 interview that he had been diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome.[841]
<info> American actor David Howard Thornton, known for playing Art the Clown in the Terrifier franchise, spoke in a 2023 interview about discovering he is autistic as an adult.[842]
<info> Quiet influence: the introvert's guide to making a difference[843] by American counsellor Jennifer B. Kahnweiler,[844] was released in 2013.

<info> Speech therapist Barry Prizant (one of the SCERTS authors),[845] released a popular book in August 2015 - Uniquely Human: A Different Way of Seeing Autism. The book explains autism from a neurodiversity perspective. A new edition was published in 2022,[846] with the help of writer Tom Fields-Meyer.[847]
<info> The ABA Visual Language: Applied Behavior Analysis by Japanese ABA practitioner Makoto Shibutani, was published in May 2017.[848]

<info> ABA book Positive Parenting for Autism: Powerful Strategies to Help Your Child Overcome Challenges and Thrive was released by American speech therapist Victoria Boone[849] in December 2018.[850]
<info> Autobiography Autism in Heels: The Untold Story of a Female Life on the Spectrum was released by American writer Jennifer Cook O'Toole in December 2018.[851]

<info> A book to help children, Can You See Me?, was released by the Americans Libby Scott (autistic child)[852] and Rebecca Westcott (special school teacher)[853] in August 2019. Three sequels have followed.
<info> A book to help non-autistic people communicate with autistic ones, Connecting With The Autism Spectrum, was released by Dutch-Canadian autistic artist Casey Vormer in October 2020.[854]

<info> Divergent Mind: Thriving in a World That Wasn't Designed for You was released by American journalist Jenara Nerenberg in February 2021.[855] It explores how ADHD, autism, synaesthesia, high sensitivity, and sensory processing disorder manifest in women.
<info> ABA book Turn Autism Around: An Action Guide for Parents of Young Children with Early Signs of Autism was released in March 2022 by American nurse Mary Barbera.[856]
<info> Unmasking Autism: Discovering the New Faces of Neurodiversity was a popular book written by American psychologist Devon Price, and published in April 2022.[857]
<info> What I Mean When I Say I'm Autistic: Unpuzzling a Life on the Autism Spectrum[858] was an autobiography released by American writer Annie Kotowicz in October 2022.[859]
<info> Autobiography Strong Female Character was released by autistic Scottish comedian Fern Brady in January 2024.[860]
<info> Autism: A Social and Medical History[861] was published by Dutch autism researcher Mitzi Waltz in 2013. (A second edition was published in 2023.)
<info> The Encyclopedia of Autism Spectrum Disorders was first published in 2013.[862] Its chief editor was American psychiatrist Fred Volkmar. (A second edition was published in 2021).[863]

<info> Bestseller NeuroTribes: The Legacy of Autism and the Future of Neurodiversity was published by American writer Steve Silberman in August 2015. It did much to spread the concept of neurodiversity, and explain the history of autism.

<info> In a Different Key: The Story of Autism by American journalists John Donvan and Caren Zucker[864] was released in January 2016. The book was a finalist for a 2017 Pulitzer Prize. It was adapted into a documentary movie released in 2021.[865]
<info> The Metamorphosis of Autism: A History of Child Development in Britain[866] was released by British health historian Bonnie Evans[867] in 2017.
<info> Asperger's Children: The Origins of Autism in Nazi Vienna[868] was released by American historian Edith Sheffer[869] in May 2018.
<info> Our autistic lives: personal accounts from autistic adults aged 20 to 70+[870] was compiled by British autism writer Alex Ratcliffe,[871] and was released in January 2020.[872]
